Open npm outdated on any project older than six months. Run uv lock --check on the backend. Look at the base image tag in your Dockerfile. You already know what you'll find. Things behind. entry.title: My Experience Building My First Token And Having it Exist On-Chain.
entry.summary: There’s something quietly satisfying about seeing a token you built from scratch exist on-chain. Not just a random mint address… Today made Solana feel a lot more real to me. What fascinates me most is how blockchain simplifies things that would normally require a full backend system in Web2. In a traditional app, you would create database tables for balances, build APIs for transfers, manage metadata, and maintain servers to keep everything running. But on Solana, the protocol already provides the structure. The mint becomes the definition of the currency. Except this time, everything is transparent and verifiable on-chain. I also explored Token Extensions metadata today, and I love the idea of storing metadata directly inside the mint account itself. Fewer moving parts, fewer accounts, lower costs, and a cleaner design overall. Still learning.

entry.title: Should Websites Allow AI Search Crawlers?
entry.summary: Should websites allow AI search crawlers? Not blindly. Blocking every AI crawler can protect content from some forms of reuse, but it can also make a site less visible in AI answers, citations, and assistant workflows. Allowing every AI crawler can increase exposure, but it can also let AI systems summarize the content without sending traffic back. The better question is: Which crawler should be allowed, for which purpose, on which content? That matters because "AI crawler" is not one category. A crawler may be used for: Search indexing AI answer grounding Model training User-triggered fetching Agent or enterprise workflows Those are different use cases. entry.title: Chunking Strategies for AI Code Review on Large Repos
entry.summary:
i spent the last few days building an open-source AI code reviewer called Basira. one of the hardest design problems was figuring out how to feed entire github repos to an LLM without blowing past the context window or burning the budget. here's what i landed on. a medium repo is 50-200 files, 5-50k lines. claude sonnet has a 200k token context window, but stuffing the whole repo in is wasteful: most files don't need review at the same time, and the model loses focus on a wall of unrelated code. One file per call: explodes API costs and loses cross-file context. an issue in auth.py might depend on a model defined in users.py.
